Question: Which novel is recommended to read first: The Foundation Trilogy or Dune?
Old_Answer: I would say you could read them in either order. Foundation is significantly shorter, and made up of short stories. Dune is more of a classic adventure story with an exotic location and strange alien life. Foundation is mostly conversations, frequently about how violence is stupid. I think thematically they are complimentary. Foundation is a series about an empire in terminal decline and the creation of the foundation on which its eventual replacement will rest. It’s extremely philosophical, with its often stated theme being that “Violence is the last refuge of the incompetent.” The characters always discover better ways to secure their goals than violence. There are stories about the use of religion and economics instead of conquest. The principle driving Foundation is that the actions driving groups of people is predictable, and because of this there is a path that, once set in motion, will be hard to deviate from. Dune is a series about a messianic figure appearing in the desert who takes control over the resource all transportation is based on. It is, much like Foundation, very philosophical. But it has more traditional action/adventure elements, such as wars and interpersonal fights. Dune is also interested in religion and economics, but comes to very different conclusions (and sometimes very similar) conclusions. Dune is also very concerned with fate and destiny, with psychic visions driving the entire series’ narrative. Like I said, they are more complimentary than competitive. I don’t think there is anything wrong with picking either series to start with. They are both good. They are both foundational sci-fi texts. If someone were to ask me this in real life, I would ask them what kind of sci-fi they like, if it is Star Wars, then Dune, if it is Star Trek, then Foundation. But that’s incredibly simplistic and reductive. Just in general, I would probably say Dune, as the first novel is largely what a person would expect from a sci-fi novel, while Foundation is very much its own thing. But read them both! I did, and I turned out fine!

Foundation, which began as a series of short stories, focuses on the grand sweep of history and the concept of psychohistory—mathematics applied to the prediction of future events. The themes are deeply rooted in politics, sociology, and the ebb and flow of civilizations, making it a cerebral journey that often feels more like an exploration of ideas than of characters. In stark contrast, Dune immerses you in the richly detailed world of Arrakis, where ecological themes, individual destiny, and personal power play critical roles. Herbert's writing is lush and filled with intricate character development, not to mention a compelling narrative that feels intensely personal amidst the grand stakes. If you prefer a more idea-driven narrative that examines societal trends and the impact of individual actions on a cosmic scale, Foundation may be the way to go. However, if you’re drawn to deeply personal stories with strong characters and a complex world-building experience, then Dune is your destination. Ultimately, you cannot go wrong with either choice, but I would lean toward starting with Dune for its engaging storytelling that draws you into its world while still offering profound themes to ponder as you read.

Question: How come no X-Men or Fantastic Four characters appear in the video game Lego Marvel Super Heroes 2, unlike the first Lego Marvel Super Heroes game?
Old_Answer: In the mid-2010s, when the MCU was cresting to its peak, real life super villian Ike Perlmutter got irrationally angry at Fox, believing they owed Marvel (and thus him) money. “Owed” is a much stronger word than is accurate, Fox was following all the contracts it had signed with Marvel when it bought the film rights to the X-Men and the Fantastic Four. Perlmutter simply believed the rights were under sold, and so he deserved more money. Perlmutter was the CEO of Marvel, and thus it was in his power to kill the X-Men and the Fantastic Four stone cold dead as brands. Perlmutter's motivation seems to be that if he did as much damage to those two brands as he could, then Fox would be willing to renegotiate the contracts. So Marvel entered a period where the X-Men and Fantastic Four were persona non gratta by Marvel. There has always been a rumor that Perlmutter went into the Marvel offices and saw someone with a Fantastic Four poster on their cubicle and he ripped it down and then ripped it up in front of them. Normally I am not one to give much credence to rumors, but that story is in line with every other story I have heard about Perlmutter. There is a long list of news items that came out over those years about the X-Men and Fantastic Four being dropped as characters. And in a rare spirit of unanimity, CBR also confirmed that the Fantastic Four comics were to go on "hiatus". Mondo Posters confirmed they were unable to make Fantastic Four posters anymore. Gazillion execs say they got in trouble for including the Fantastic Four in Marvel Heroes game update. The Marvel Heroes ID posters lost the X-Men and the Fantastic Four. Statue lines featuring the Fantastic Four or the X-Men were cancelled in mid-sculpt. Trading cards could no longer be reprinted. Fantastic Four was snubbed in 'Marvel's Greatest Collections'. They were not part of the Star Wars Welcome Home posters. There were no Fantastic Four or X-Men T-shirts anymore, and such characters were removed from group shots. Marvel pulled permission for an art show — but only for the Fantastic Four characters. Foreign comics saw Fantastic Four characters removed from strips, and it was confirmed to me that Panini was not allowed to publish translated Fantastic Four comics. This all culminated in the straight up cancelation of the Fantastic Four comic. But in this period there were no toys, no cartoons, and no video games. Marvel strictly forbid its licensees from using those two properties. I will also say that Marvel spent this entire time period lying. I don’t think I have ever seen a corporation put so much effort into gaslighting its own customers as Marvel did. Marvel had many, many employees insist that this wasn’t happening and that the fans of the X-Men and Fantastic Four were being paranoid for claiming it was. Tom Brevoort, who is about to become the X-Men editor, straight up lied to retailers claiming the Fantastic Four comic was not going to be canceled only a few months prior to the announcement it was canceled. I have an extraordinary degree of contempt for him. Lego Marvel Superheroes comes out in 2013, and is filled with X-Men and Fantastic Four characters. Nearly thirty playable characters are from those two franchises, and the mansion and the Baxter Building are both important locations. Lego Marvel Superheroes 2 comes out in 2017 and there are zero. And, wow, the game developers made some deep cuts to fill out the games roster, making the absences that much more obvious. No Storm or Thing, but it does have Arizona Girl, a character from Wild West #1 in 1948 and only has ten appearances in her entire existence. Surely you are aware of beloved Marvel character Arizona Girl and are excited to see her in a video game as opposed to a minor character like *checks notes* someone named “Doctor Doom.” Given the development cycle for video games, I bet Lego Marvel Superheroes was one of the last times Marvel agreed to let a licensee use those characters. But, since we are talking about video games and Marvel declaring the X-Men and Fantastic Four forbidden, the absolute most bananas example was Marvel vs. Capcom Infinite. Where Capcom’s people were stuck trying to explain why characters who had been in every incarnation of the franchise were not included without just saying Marvel was out of its gourd. There was recently a leak about the characters, and people picked up on the fact that a lot of classic characters aren't there, specifically the X-Men characters like Magneto and Sentinel. How do you guys feel about people being hung up on that? Peter Rosas: If you were to actually think about it, these characters are just functions. They're just doing things. Magneto, case and point, is a favorite because he has eight-way dash and he's really fast, right? So our more technical players, all they want to do is triangle jump and that kind of stuff. Well guess what, Nova can do the same thing, Captain Marvel can do the same thing. Ultron can do the same thing. Go ahead and try them out. It's just the function that people are associating with the character, and there's no shortage of that. We made sure that all proper play styles can be represented with our current roster. The design team has been looking at that very closely. We wanted to make sure that if a legacy character doesn't happen to make the roster this time, that play style would still be represented. That somebody who has associated themselves with Magneto wouldn't be lost coming into this title. Michael Evans: The other thing is, you mentioned returning characters right? If you look at the returning characters and you play with them, you'll notice that they're quite different from their previous iterations. Iron Man, he plays completely different. He has new special moves. Obviously we wanted to keep fan-favorite characters, but since you have the new system they're gonna play differently. In addition to that, new special moves, new hypers, new level threes in some cases, these breathe new life into these characters even if they are returning. So we did definitely make an attempt to do that. The X-Men stuff, [I] can't talk to. But I do want to talk about the character-selection process because I think it's important. There's three things we're looking at: Gameplay first and foremost of course. The Capcom R&D team and us, we get together and we talk with Marvel about what characters we want to put in. From a character-type perspective, we want our big brawler characters, our characters that can fly, our small characters or whatever. Just from a creative side, gameplay, here's the characters we want. That plays a part. One of the first things we did was sit down to write the story. When we were thinking about the story we wanted to tell, as fans ourselves on both sides, on the Marvel side there's Mike Jones, an ex-Capcom guy. We're big Marvel fans, so we're sitting down to just like, "What crazy interactions do we want to see? What would happen if Docket, Dante, and Rocket came together? What would happen and who are these pairings that we want to see?" So from a storytelling perspective that also played into the character selection. Then the third one is obviously the popularity of these characters. X was one we had to get in there. A lot of fans wanted to see X, so we brought him back. Then also we talked with Marvel very closely about their future roadmap, about what's gonna be happening. Your modern Marvel fan, maybe they don't even remember some of the X-Men characters, but they know some of the Guardians characters or Black Panther. You know what I mean? Captain Marvel may seem like a strange pick, but she's fantastic. She fits the gameplay. She fits the story, and they're gonna be really pushing her as a strong female lead all the way up into the movie. We're trying to take everything into account and choose the best characters. The characters are just functions, man. They do stuff on the screen, like dash! Capcom is spending all this money to license these characters from Marvel because you can’t, like, make a stick figure that dashes. And any wany, obviously no one even remembers the X-Men in the first place. This remains one of the most ludicrous examples of corporate human speak I have ever seen. Any way, that’s why the X-Men and the Fantastic Four were missing.

Question: What's up with all these New Gay movies?
Old_Answer: I have seen sixteen movies this year and only five of them have any gay content at all: Mean Girls, Monkey Man, Challengers, The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare, and Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes. And some of these are extreme stretches. Truly extremely stretches. In the adaptation of the musical Broadway adaptation of the 2004 film Mean Girls, the character Damian is openly gay just like he was in the original film. Additionally in this version Janis is also a lesbian, and this is a fairly important plot point with regards to her falling out with Regina George. But, if you are see the movie adaptation or the Broadway play adaptation of 2004 teen comedy that already included gay characters… then it should not be super surprising that there are gay characters in the film. In this revenge film set in India, the main character, who is unnamed but calls himself “Bobby” at times, is saved from drowning in a river after his first attempt at revenge goes wrong by Alpha, the keeper of Ardhanarishvara, a local temple whose hijra community is being targeted by the police/politicians. Ardhanarishvara is a form of the Hindu deity Shiva combined with his consort Parvati. Ardhanarishvara is depicted as half-male and half-female, equally split down the middle. Hijra would be the equivalent of transgender, intersex, and eunuch people. Bobby heals at their temple, spiritually and physically, and trains there too, again spiritually and physically. And then gets them the money they need to continue to exist. And, in the end, they help him with his revenge. This is all stuff that is extremely specific to India, and all pretty fascinating. It is a look into a culture that most Americans are unaware of. If you don’t know that this is a film by the director of Call Me By Your Name, then I can see someone going to see the Zendaya tennis movie and being very confused by the product they are watching. My friend went to see it with her grandmother and reported that, yes, it was awkward. It’s a film about three tennis players, a men’s pair and a female prodigy, who spend the entire film wanting to have sex with each other in every possible combination. And Patrick and Art, the two men in the film, do make out while Zendaya watches. If you think this is a tennis movie and not a movie where tennis is a metaphor for sex, then I can see being surprised. The team behind the film does try to prepare audiences for what they are going to see by putting “Luca Guadagnino’s Challengers” in all the advertising… but what percentage of the population are going to realize he directed Call Me By Your Name? Also both Art and Patrick spend the whole movie having sex with Zendaya. It’s a single exchange: Gus: If that’s how you fight, I’d hate to see you love. Anders: You don’t have to worry about that, you’re too pretty for me. Freddy, on the other hand… Freddy: You’d have to catch me first. Anders: I do love to hunt. Freddy: You’d be lucky. Anders: I’m really getting quite hot. It is… unclear if this is supposed to be taken as a literal confirmation of a character’s sexual orientation or a joke between a bunch of guys who like killin’ Nazis. Or possibly both? They’re laughing the entire time they are saying these lines. It’s a fifteen second gay joke in a film where a huge portion of the film is spent on a female spy seducing a Nazi. The chimpanzee protagonist Noa crashes into the home of orangutan Raka. Raka is, at the moment, holding a funeral for his partner in the Order of Caesar, who he refers to as “his tribe.” That’s it, it’s like four words. Four ambiguous words. There are some soldiers in Civil War that you could maybe think are indicated to not be straight. I’m sure there is something in Lisa Frankenstein I am forgetting. And at the very least Argyle can be interpreted as having gay elements. The idea that there’s “all these new gay movies” is just not true. In the pre-summer blockbuster period of the year, when all the art films are released, it’s still only like a third of films have a gay character at all, and half of those are just ambiguous lines of dialogue.
